tip: Two whys: 'por qué' asks the cause, 'para qué' asks the purpose. '¿Para qué sirve esto?' = what is this FOR – swap them and you're asking the wrong question.
In 'ponlo', the pronoun 'lo' attaches to the affirmative command – it goes at the end as one word.
'Podrías' = could you? Conditional of 'poder' for polite requests. '¿Podrías ayudarme?' Softer than '¿Puedes...?'
'Espero que' + subjunctive: hoping about someone else's action triggers subjunctive. 'Espero que vengas' (I hope you come).
'Me alegro de que' + present perfect subjunctive.
You don't hit someone in Spanish – you hit TO them: 'pegarle a tu hermana' needs 'le' + 'a', as if delivering the blow. 'Pegar' treats its victim as an indirect object.
'Es importante que' + subjunctive: impersonal value judgments trigger subjunctive. 'Es importante que estudies.'
'Puede que' + subjunctive = maybe/it's possible: 'Puede que venga' (He might come). Possibility → subjunctive.
No if-clause required: 'yo en tu lugar' (me, in your place) + conditional 'buscaría' does the whole 'if I were you' job. Spanish skips the 'si' entirely.
Strangers get flipped-vowel orders: 'usted' commands like 'siga' and 'gire' (from 'sigue'/'gira'). Directions from officials and shopkeepers normally come in this shape.
'Para que' + subjunctive = so that: 'Hablo despacio para que entiendas.' Purpose involving another person → subjunctive.
'A menos que' always takes subjunctive.
'No creo que' + subjunctive – negated belief triggers subjunctive.
Even hard facts take subjunctive: 'el hecho de que no haya venido' – it really happened, but Spanish marks it as reacted-to, not newly asserted.
'What' meaning 'the thing that' is 'lo que': 'lo que quiero saber' = the-thing-that I want to know. Save 'qué' for questions, asked or reported ('dime qué...').
'En caso de que' + subjunctive = in case.
'Se celebrará' isn't about a party: 'celebrar' also means to hold (a meeting, elections, a trial). Here the 'reunión de seguimiento' will simply take place next Monday.
Odd pair: 'go!' is 'vete', but 'don't go' isn't 'no te vete' – negative commands switch to subjunctive, so it's 'no te vayas'. The pronoun 'te' also jumps back in front.
'Aunque llueva' = even if it rains (maybe it won't). 'Aunque llueve' = even though it's raining (it is). One vowel tells you whether the rain is real or hypothetical.
'Para mí' = in my opinion: 'Para mí, es mejor así.' 'Para' + person for personal viewpoint.
English strands prepositions (the restaurant we went TO); Spanish never does. The 'a' jumps up front: 'al que fuimos'. Saying 'que fuimos a' sounds foreign.
'Lo lejos que estemos' – Spanish packages 'how far' as 'lo' + adverb + 'que', and 'no matter' forces subjunctive 'estemos': the distance is left open, not stated.
Bare imperatives are polite bar Spanish: 'Ponme una caña' (put me a small draft beer) is standard, not bossy. A could-you-possibly order sounds oddly stiff in Spain.
The vase trap: flowers go in a 'jarrón', never a 'vaso' – 'vaso' is a drinking glass. Ask for a 'vaso' for your roses and you'll get a tumbler of water.
'El quinto piso' is the US sixth floor: Spanish numbering starts above the 'planta baja' (ground floor). Five full flights with no 'ascensor' – count accordingly.
They really didn't tell – yet it's 'hayan dicho', subjunctive. Emotion verbs like 'molestar' trigger it even for true facts: you're reacting, not reporting.
Spanish builds 'whatever he does' by echoing the verb: 'haga lo que haga', literally 'do what he may do'. Works with any verb – 'diga lo que diga', whatever he says.
'Haga' is subjunctive for 'yo' AND 'él/ella/usted', so 'haga lo que haga' could mean 'whatever I do' or 'whatever he does' – the form alone can't tell you; context has to.
'Tocar' is an '-ar' verb, yet the command is 'toque': 'usted' commands flip to the opposite vowel ('-ar' takes '-e', '-er/-ir' take '-a'). That vowel swap IS the subjunctive.
Command someone to do it and pronouns glue onto the verb: 'dímelo'. Say don't and they leap in front: 'no me lo digas'. Negation always pulls pronouns before the verb.
